faq.a: Galvanising is coating steel with zinc to stop it rusting. In hot-dip galvanising, cleaned steel is dipped in molten zinc, which bonds to it. You see it on crash barriers, lamp posts, nails and buckets.
Iron in steel reacts with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron oxide, rust. Rust is crumbly and lets more water through, so steel keeps rusting deeper unless it is protected. Salt speeds it up.

faq.q: Why is a galvanised coating so tough?
faq.a: The zinc does not just sit on top like paint: it reacts with the steel to form layers of zinc-iron alloy that are bonded into the surface and are even harder than the steel, so knocks rarely chip it off.

faq.q: Why doesn't scratched galvanised steel rust?
faq.a: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so where both are exposed to water, the zinc corrodes instead of the iron. It sacrifices itself to protect the bare steel, a trick called sacrificial or cathodic protection.
A typical hot-dip coating can protect steel for 50 years or more in a dry rural area, but less near the sea or in polluted air, where salt and acid wear the zinc away faster.

facts: Hot-dip galvanising baths are kept at about 450 °C.
Galvanising is named after Luigi Galvani; Stanislas Sorel patented hot-dip galvanising in France in 1837.
